# Climbing Kilimanjaro: a 20-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 27 October 2026 from 45 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

A multi-day trek to 5,895 m (19,341 ft) with a licensed operator; summit day is long, cold and at high altitude. [1, 2]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [3, 4]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 5, 6]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [7, 8, 9]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [3, 10, 11]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [9, 12]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 9]
- Train for the ground you will cover. For hill challenges walk hills fast, or use stairs, and add short hill repeats of 50 to 100 metres of climb, four to six times, coming down slowly. [1, 2]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [3, 9, 13]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 5, 6, 14]
- In the later weeks, train with the pack and the kit you will carry on the day so nothing is new. [1, 2, 15]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [9, 16, 17, 18]
- Before a multi-day trip, practise long days back to back, such as a long walk on Saturday and another on Sunday, so you know how your body copes with the second day. [13, 19]
- Build your training walks from a few miles up to a full day's distance, carrying the pack you will use. [2, 15]

*Hill repeats*: climb a steep hill or stairs for 50 to 100 metres of height, four to six times, coming down slowly. [1, 2]

## What each part of the plan is for

- **The Saturday long hill walk with your pack.** The long session prepares you for the length of the day itself. Its pace does not matter; covering the time or distance does, so keep it at a conversational effort. [1, 2, 9]
- **The easy brisk walk or cross-trainings.** Easy sessions add fitness without leaving you too tired for the long session. Top endurance athletes do about four in five of their sessions at this low effort. [7, 8]
- **Hill repeats.** Hill repeats practise exactly what a hill challenge asks of you, climbing again and again, then coming down slowly and with control. [1, 2]
- **Strength and balance.** Strength and balance work is what keeps you in one piece. In trials it cut sports injuries to about a third, it is part of the official guidance for everyone on at least two days a week, and core and balance work helps on rough ground. [2, 5, 14]
- **Rest days.** Rest days are when your body recovers from the work and adapts to it. The NHS's beginner running plan puts a rest day between every run. [3, 12]
- **Easier weeks.** An easier week every third week lets the tiredness of the previous weeks clear, so your fitness can rebound before you build again. [9, 12]
- **Carrying your pack.** Training with your loaded pack matches the conditions of the day and shows you what you really need to carry. [2, 15]
- **The taper.** Cutting back in the final weeks lets your muscles recover and your body refuel, so you arrive fresh rather than tired. In research, a two-week taper improved performance. [16, 17]

## Each week, and why

**Week 1: setting the pattern.**

- Five sessions and two rest days. The long hill walk with your pack starts at 4 hours.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 9]
- Tuesday's easy brisk walk or cross-training: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 5, 14]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [3, 12]

**Week 2: building.**

- The long hill walk with your pack grows to 4 hours, up from 4 hours in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [3, 10, 11]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 5, 14]

**Week 3: an easier week.**

- The long hill walk with your pack eases back to 3.5 hours.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [9, 12]
- New this week, hill repeats on Thursday: it practises the climbing and the controlled descents the challenge is made of [1, 2]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [3, 12]

## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [5, 6, 14]
- Squat-type exercises are the backbone of leg and hip strength. Start with sit-to-stand and mini-squats, adding repetitions gradually, then move on to squats and lunges, with core work for balance on rough ground. [2, 20]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 14]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [5]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [13, 17]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [3, 17]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 5, 6, 14, 20]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 21]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [17, 21]
- Train in the footwear you will use on the day and break new shoes in gradually. Wear moisture-wicking socks and change them if your feet sweat. [13, 17, 22]
- Deal with a hot spot as soon as you feel it. Cover a blister with a soft or padded plaster and do not burst it; get advice if it shows signs of infection. [13, 22]

## On the day

- Carry a map and compass and know how to use them; do not rely on signs or a phone, whose signal and battery can fail. [1, 2]
- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [7, 17]
- On a multi-day trip keep the first few days shorter while you find your rhythm, let the daily distance flex with the terrain and how you feel, and build in easier days or full rest days. [13, 15]

## Safety

- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [23]
- Check the forecast, walk in daylight, leave your route with someone, and turn back if conditions get beyond you. Summits are colder than valleys. [1]
- Above 3,000 metres, sleep no more than 500 metres higher than the night before and take a rest day at the same height every three or four days. Avoid going from below 1,200 metres to above 3,500 metres in a day. [4, 24, 25]
- Being fit does not protect you from altitude sickness. Choose an itinerary with acclimatisation days and climb slowly however strong you feel. [4, 25]
- Headache with nausea, dizziness or tiredness can be altitude sickness. Stop climbing and rest; if it gets worse or has not improved after a day, go down. Confusion, poor balance, breathlessness at rest or a wet cough are emergencies; descend at once and get help. [4, 24]
- See your GP or a travel clinic before a high-altitude trip, especially if you have a health condition or have had altitude sickness before; they can discuss preventive medicine. Make sure your insurance covers evacuation. [4, 24]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [26]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [3, 17]
